opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most exciting things about the approach. The basic idea behind parameter decomposition is that instead of looking at a network's activations and trying to find directions that correspond to features, we decompose the network's *weights* into a set of components. Each component is a piece of the mechanism the network uses, and the goal is that on any given input only a small number of those components are actually needed to reproduce the network's behavior. So you're looking for a description of the computation that is faithful to the original parameters, minimal, and simple.

Why does that help with extracting knowledge? A lot of what a model "knows" isn't stored in any single activation. It's stored in the weights: the transformations the model applies, the associations it has learned, the algorithms it has picked up during training. Activation-based methods like sparse autoencoders give you a dictionary of the *variables* the network represents, but they don't tell you as directly what the network is *doing* with those variables. Parameter decomposition tries to get at the mechanisms themselves. If you can isolate a component that, for example, implements a particular factual association or a particular step of some algorithm, then you've pulled out a piece of knowledge in a form you can actually inspect.

There are a few things I find especially promising here. The first is that it gives you a natural unit of analysis that lives in the same space as the model itself. Components are parameter vectors, so you can ablate them, edit them, or study how they interact, and you're intervening on the real mechanism rather than on a proxy. The second is that it potentially sidesteps some problems we've run into with activation-based approaches, like feature splitting, or the sense that the dictionary you get depends heavily on the dataset and dictionary size. If the network really does implement a fixed set of mechanisms, then in principle there's a more canonical decomposition to find. The third is that it points toward a world where interpretability is less about labeling neurons or directions and more about reading out the learned algorithms. That's closer to what we actually want if the aim is to learn things *from* models, not just about them.

Now, I want to be honest that we're still early. The methods are expensive. Scaling them to large models is a real research challenge, and there are open questions about whether the decompositions we find are the "right" ones, as opposed to just one of many valid ones. But the long-term vision, and the reason I'm excited, is this: as models get better than us at certain things, say in science or medicine, they'll have learned structure in the world that we don't yet understand. If we can decompose them into their constituent mechanisms, we have a shot at actually extracting that understanding and bringing it back into human knowledge. That's not just a safety story. It could be a genuinely new way of doing science.

r001.rationale: The response proposes decomposing the network’s weights into inspectable mechanism components to extract learned associations and algorithms, describing this as working in the model’s own parameter space.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the fundamental problem in interpretability is that we don't have a good notion of what the "parts" of a neural network are. A network is just a big pile of parameters, and when you want to ask "what does this network know, and how does it do what it does," you need some way to carve it into pieces that correspond to the actual computations it's performing. For a long time the default unit was the neuron, and then with sparse autoencoders the unit became directions in activation space. Both of those are really about activations, though, about what the network represents on a given input. Parameter decomposition is trying to go one level deeper and ask: what are the mechanisms, written in the weights, that produce those representations?

The basic idea is that you take the parameters of the network and you try to decompose them into a sum of components, where each component is a vector in parameter space, and you want the components to have a few properties. One is that if you add them all back up, you get the original network, so you're being faithful to what the model actually does. Another is that on any given input, only a small number of those components should be necessary to reproduce the network's behavior, so they're used sparsely. And a third is that each component should be as simple as possible, ideally something like low rank, so it's doing one thing rather than being a tangled bundle of many things.

If you can get that to work, and I'll say up front that it's early days and we've mostly demonstrated it on toy models and small transformers, then I think it gives you a very different handle on knowledge extraction than we've had before. Right now if you want to know what a model knows about, say, some factual relationship, you basically have to probe it behaviorally. You ask it questions and look at the outputs, or you look at activations on specific inputs and try to find features. But that's always conditional on the inputs you thought to try. With a parameter decomposition, in principle the components are the knowledge. They're the mechanisms sitting there in the weights whether or not you've run the right input through the network. So you could imagine enumerating the components, looking at what each one does, and building up a picture of what the model is capable of that isn't bottlenecked on your imagination about what prompts to write.

The other thing I find exciting is that it connects more naturally to the compressed nature of what networks learn. Networks are doing superposition, they're packing more mechanisms into the weights than there are dimensions, and a lot of what makes them hard to understand is that these mechanisms are overlapping in confusing ways. A decomposition that's designed around sparsity and simplicity is explicitly trying to pull those overlapping mechanisms apart. So you'd get something closer to a parts list for the model, where each part is a piece of learned structure, rather than a parts list for the hardware, which is what neurons give you.

There's a long way to go from here to extracting, say, novel scientific knowledge from a frontier model. The methods have to scale, we need to deal with the fact that the components we find aren't always as clean as we'd like, and there's a hard question about how you go from "here's a component" to "here's a human-understandable statement about what it does." But I think the conceptual move, from decomposing activations to decomposing the computation itself, is the right one, and it's the kind of thing that could eventually let us read knowledge off a network directly rather than inferring it from behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says parameter decomposition could expose the mechanisms in the weights and that its components are, in principle, the model’s knowledge, which could be enumerated to understand what the model knows.

astra-6.text:
The hope is that parameter decomposition gives us a way to understand the knowledge encoded in a network’s weights. Those weights are available to us, but they’re not written in a language we can readily understand. And an individual weight generally isn’t going to correspond to a single, meaningful piece of knowledge.

So the idea is to decompose the parameters into components that correspond to coherent pieces of computation. If we can identify what each component does, and how those components interact, then we might be able to translate some of the network’s internal structure into something humans can understand.

There’s an important distinction here between eliciting knowledge by asking a model questions and extracting it by examining the mechanisms that produce its answers. With the latter, you could potentially uncover things the model doesn’t reliably articulate when prompted. You could also intervene on a component to test whether your interpretation actually explains the model’s behavior.

But decomposition alone doesn’t solve that problem. You still need to establish that the components are meaningful, interpret them correctly, and validate those interpretations. So I see it as a possible foundation for knowledge extraction, rather than a method that automatically turns weights into a list of facts.

r001.rationale: The response proposes decomposing weights into interpretable computational components, but does not clearly say this accesses knowledge in the network’s own conceptual terms; it frames the goal as translating internal structure into human-understandable form.

sol-6.1.text:
The hope is that parameter decomposition gives us a way to break a network down into pieces that correspond to meaningful parts of its computation. The knowledge is encoded in the weights, but it’s distributed across them, so looking at individual parameters doesn’t tell you very much.

If we can find components that implement particular features or mechanisms, we can start asking what each one does, which other components it interacts with, and under what circumstances it matters. You might identify a component that represents some relationship, then intervene on it to test whether that interpretation actually explains the model’s behavior.

I wouldn’t expect a decomposition to immediately hand us a list of facts in English. There’s still a substantial interpretation problem. But it could give us a more useful unit of analysis—a bridge between the numerical weights and an explanation of what the network has learned.

r001.rationale: The response says decomposition can reveal components that implement meaningful features or mechanisms, providing a way to understand learned knowledge in terms of the network’s own internal structure.
